# Should gear shift center itself while in neutral?

In a manual transmission, the behavior of the shifter when placed in neutral isn't merely a matter of convenience; it is a direct result of how the mechanical linkage and internal springs are balanced. Your 2001 Mitsubishi Eclipse exhibiting a shifter that sticks to the left or right rather than returning to center is not a defect in the logic of the system, but it does indicate a deviation from the factory tuning found in many other vehicles, like your previous Mazda RX-7.

The mechanical reality is that most manual transmissions do not inherently possess a strong "return-to-center" force for every gear position. Instead, they rely on the geometry of the shift forks and the tension of specific springs to hold the selector rod or cable in place. When you engage neutral, the mechanism relies on these springs to settle into a resting position. If the shifter feels like it is crawling slowly toward center or sticking firmly to one side, it suggests that the internal spring tension has weakened over time or that there is excess play within the linkage.

In the context of your Eclipse, the lack of immediate centering is likely due to worn bushings in the shift linkage or a fatigued spring pack inside the transmission housing. Unlike the 1979 Mazda RX-7, which was engineered with a robust return mechanism that facilitated effortless shifting between gears like third and fourth, modern and even some contemporary manual cars often rely on friction plates or tighter tolerances to maintain position. The "stickiness" you are experiencing is a physical manifestation of these components losing their original specification.

Restoring the crisp centering action involves inspecting the external linkage first before considering internal disassembly. The process begins by identifying the pivot points and bushings connected to the shifter lever. Over decades of use, rubber grommets and plastic bushings can degrade, introducing slop into the system. This slop prevents the selector from finding a precise neutral position, causing it to drift. Replacing these external components is often the most cost-effective solution. It requires locating the specific bushing kits for your model year and replacing them with high-quality replacements that restore the original pivot geometry.

If the external linkage is in good condition, the issue may reside inside the transmission case. The selector shafts and forks are held by springs that provide the necessary tension. These springs can lose their elasticity or break entirely. Accessing these requires removing the transmission from the vehicle to disassemble the mainshaft and inspect the internal components. This is a significantly more involved procedure than swapping bushings. You would need to carefully extract the old springs, measure their dimensions against factory specifications, and install new ones that match the original tension rating.

There is a trade-off here between effort and outcome. Simply replacing parts might restore the centering action, but it does not address the wear on the metal shafts themselves. If the shafts have rounded edges from years of movement, new springs may not be enough to force the shifter back to center reliably. A thorough inspection of the internal gears and forks is mandatory if you choose this route.

Ultimately, while it is normal for different cars to have varying shift feel profiles, a shifter that sticks or crawls significantly impacts driving confidence, particularly when upshifting from third to fourth in traffic. Restoring the factory-feel spring action is achievable but requires distinguishing between simple external linkage wear and more complex internal spring failure.
